newsitem.title: GERMANY: Conference pledges to end landmine tragedy.
newsitem.headline: Conference pledges to end landmine tragedy.

text.p: Land-mine experts gathered in Bonn on Wednesday to discuss ways to clear 110 million mines that litter fields, roads and waterways around the world, a day after the U.N. voted for a global ban on anti-personnel mines.

Mechanical mine-clearing was the hot topic at the conference proposed by German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, a staunch supporter of efforts to cut the number of mines laid each year -- currently 2.5 million -- and improve clearing.

The United Nations calculates that at the current rate it will take more than 1,000 years to clear the world's mines, provided no more are laid, Kinkel said in a speech to open the two-day conference.
Meanwhile around 20,000 people are either killed or maimed by mines each year.
"Mine clearance at present is like trying to move a sand dune with a thimble. And to complete the picture, whole lorry loads of sand are constantly being tipped onto the dune," Kinkel said.
He welcomed the U.N. General Assembly vote and said mine clearing would in future be "part and parcel of U.N. peacekeeping missions".
Standing among metal detectors, plastic models and defused mines which looked surprisingly benign, equipment manufacturers showed off their machines with posters and action videos.

The Spitfire Demining System, developed by Swedish company BOA Defence AB and Caterpillar, uses standard construction equipment such as mechanical diggers with accessories including armoured cladding for the drivers' cabs.

The digger churns the soil in a field, detonating mines and rendering the land fit for cultivation. It is soon to be used in Israel and Lars Nylin of the company said the machines would probably be used in Bosnia as well.
"One of the most important things about demining is clearing the land, so people can do something with it, start farms or get access to water," Nylin told Reuters.

The German Krohn Mechanical Mine Clearance System was used in Mozambique in a project sponsored by Germany's Foreign Ministry. The minefields were released for farming by the Mozambican authorities after being cleared.
The machine can clear up to 30,000 sq metres of land every day compared to 10 sq metres for manual mine clearing with a metal detector.
Mechanical clearing is also far safer than the traditional method where clearers walk into minefields and risk being blown apart by plastic mines.
Mario Feltz, a diplomat at the Angolan embassy in Bonn, told Reuters the problem was very serious in Angola.
"The country has been mined for the last 30 years. There is a large area of our country which can't be used for agriculture because of the risk of mines," he said.
The Angolan government is engaged in demining operations along with support from the international community.
